highlights: Ambassador Edwin W. Pauley toured industrial centers in North Korea on a reparations mission and found no evidence of substantial equipment removals by Soviet occupation authorities.
The Soviet Consulate in Seoul was officially closed, and its personnel, headed by Vice-Consul Alexander S. Poliansky, returned to Moscow.
Moderate leaders Dr. Kim Kyu-sik and Lyuh Woon-hyung met to negotiate a center coalition between moderate Left and Right factions after the Joint American-Soviet Commission adjourned.
The National Economic Board was established under Ordinance No. 90 to coordinate economic policy, price stabilization, commodity allocations, and rationing.
Late June flooding along the Han River caused 88 deaths and destroyed 13,686 homes, aggravating South Korea's critical summer food deficit.
Authorities contained a cholera epidemic that caused 651 deaths, administering more than 1.6 million inoculations across Seoul, Pusan, and Taegu.
About 55,000 tons of American wheat arrived to supplement depleted government rice stocks in critical deficit areas.
Masan Tuberculosis Sanatorium opened, college courses were extended to four years, and cumulative repatriation of Koreans reached nearly one million.

summary: Summation No. 9 chronicles United States Army Military Government activities in South Korea during June 1946, a month characterized by acute administrative reorganization, environmental crises, and political realignment following the adjournment of the Joint American-Soviet Commission. Major political developments include Ambassador Edwin W. Pauley's reparations inspection tour of North Korea, the closure of the Soviet Consulate in Seoul, moderate coalition initiatives led by Kim Kyu-sik and Lyuh Woon-hyung, and the creation of the National Economic Board. Catastrophic late June flooding along the Han River caused 88 deaths and devastated crops and infrastructure, compounding severe food shortages that necessitated the emergency distribution of 55,000 tons of imported American wheat. Meanwhile, military authorities vigorously combated a deadly cholera epidemic that claimed 651 lives by administering over 1.6 million inoculations. For historians, this report offers indispensable primary data, featuring detailed structural surveys of the Korean fishing industry under Japanese colonial rule, comprehensive cost-of-living and family expenditure analyses showing extreme inflation, thorough descriptions of the state monopoly bureau's operations in ginseng and tobacco, and cumulative statistics on postwar cross-border repatriation and rail rehabilitation.
